title: Power of Two
directAnswer: Return `n > 0 && (n & (n - 1)) == 0`. The positive check rules out 0 and negatives.

rules: Power of two = one set bit.
remember.takeaway: n & (n-1) == 0 (and n>0) tests for a power of two.

problemStatement: Given an integer `n`, return true if it is a power of two (1, 2, 4, 8, …), else false.
understanding: A power of two has exactly one set bit. The trick `n & (n-1) == 0` clears the lowest set bit and tests if nothing remains.

approaches.name: Clear-lowest-bit trick
approaches.whenToMention: This is the standard, expected solution — lead with it.
approaches.explanation:
A power of two has **exactly one set bit** (1, 10, 100, 1000 in binary). The trick `n & (n - 1) == 0` (with `n > 0`) tests precisely that.

**Why `n & (n-1)` clears the lowest set bit.** Subtracting 1 flips the lowest set bit to 0 and turns all bits below it to 1 (e.g. 1000 − 1 = 0111). ANDing the two leaves every bit unset *if and only if* there was a single set bit. So for a power of two the result is 0; for anything with ≥2 set bits it's non-zero.

**Why the `n > 0` guard.** 0 has no set bits and would pass `n & (n-1) == 0` falsely; negative numbers (two's complement) have many set bits but also need excluding. The positivity check rules both out.

**Why bits beat a divide loop.** Repeatedly dividing by 2 works but is O(log n) and misses the elegant single-operation insight that interviewers probe.

code.python:
def is_power_of_two(n: int) -> bool:
    return n > 0 and (n & (n - 1)) == 0

approaches.insight: `n & (n-1)` clearing the lowest set bit is one of the most reused bit tricks — also counts bits and detects powers of two.
approaches.complexityReasoning: a single subtraction and AND — constant time.

java.explanation: Positive AND only one set bit ⟹ power of two.

pitfalls: Using a loop dividing by 2 (works but misses the bit insight).

commonMistakes: Using a loop dividing by 2 (works but misses the bit insight).
patternNote: A core fresher pattern: n & (n-1) clears lowest bit. Master it on small inputs and it transfers to harder problems.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can n be 0 or negative?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Both are not powers of two — the n > 0 guard handles them.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Missing the n > 0 guard
commonMistakesDetailed.why: 0 & (0-1) == 0 is true, so without the guard zero is wrongly reported as a power of two.
